Chocolate Hills of Bohol

The Chocolate Hills are a striking geological formation of conical limestone mounds in Bohol, Philippines, famous for their chocolate-brown hue in the dry season.

Chocolate Hills

What Are the Chocolate Hills?

The Chocolate Hills are a collection of over a thousand conical limestone mounds spread across more than 50 square kilometres in Bohol. Their grass-covered surfaces turn chocolate‑brown during the dry season, giving them their name.

  • Estimated 1,260 to 1,776 individual hills
  • Located mainly in Carmen, Batuan, and Sagbayan
  • Cover an area of over 50 km²

Geology and Formation

Formed during the Late Pliocene to Early Pleistocene, the hills are karst limestone created by uplift, marine sedimentation and erosion over millions of years.

  • Late Pliocene–Early Pleistocene age
  • Karst limestone with marine fossils
  • Erosion shaped the smooth, conical forms
Timeline

History and Cultural Significance

The hills have long been a symbol of Bohol, appearing on the provincial flag and seal, and are a national geological monument.

  1. 1Declared a National Geological Monument (2000)
  2. 2Featured on Bohol’s flag and seal
  3. 3Proposed for UNESCO World Heritage status
“The Chocolate Hills are the most recognizable natural landmark of the Philippines.” – UNESCO draft

Tourism and Conservation

A major tourist draw, the hills attract visitors from around the world, while conservation efforts aim to protect them from quarrying and habitat loss.

  • Key attraction for Bohol’s tourism industry
  • Threatened by illegal quarrying
  • Protected under the Philippine Tourism Authority
